S3 does support byte-range GETs (the Range header), which is all this read-only design needs. But it does not give file-system semantics: objects are written whole, there are no in-place or random writes, renames are not supported on general purpose buckets, and the namespace is flat. AWS's own Mountpoint for S3 says it 'does not implement all the features of a POSIX file system'. Checked October 2026.
precise_version: S3 supports ranged reads (ask for n bytes at an offset and get exactly those bytes), which lets it serve this index-plus-data design, but it is an object store, not a file system: objects are written whole and cannot be modified in place.

Modern file systems allow files far larger than 1 TB: ext4 16 TiB (4 KiB blocks), NTFS 16 TB at the default 4 KB cluster (up to 8 PB), Btrfs 8 EiB in practice. Only old/simple file systems (e.g. FAT32, 4 GB) have small limits. Smaller files are mainly chosen so merge, compaction, startup and deletion work in manageable units.
precise_version: Some file systems cap file size (FAT32 at 4 GB), but modern ones allow many terabytes; the stronger reason for small files is that merge, compaction and index rebuild work file by file.

Appends approach the disk's sequential bandwidth, but every get still costs one random seek on a magnetic disk (Bitcask's guarantee is 'never more than one disk seek'), so random-read latency stays far behind SSDs. 'Almost as fast as SSDs' holds for writes, not reads.

SSDs do avoid mechanical seeks, but flash cannot be overwritten in place: it must be erased before rewriting, so random in-place updates cause garbage collection and write amplification. Sequential/append-only writes are still the flash-friendly pattern, which is why log-structured designs keep a real (smaller) benefit on SSDs.

Byte-at-a-time reads are slow, but they are not one disk I/O per byte: the kernel reads whole blocks into the page cache and serves later reads from memory, and buffered I/O libraries also read in chunks. The cost is one system/function call per byte plus the parsing, not one disk access per byte.
precise_version: Reading one byte at a time until a newline makes one call per byte (the OS page cache absorbs the disk reads), which is slow; a length-prefixed format lets you read the whole record in one go.

CRCs (Postgres uses CRC-32C per WAL record) are the standard tool for detecting accidental corruption, but not the only one: other checksums and cryptographic hashes also work, and a CRC does not protect against deliberate tampering.

Putting the CRC first is a convention (Bitcask and LevelDB do it), not a requirement. Detection works with the CRC anywhere, as long as the record length is known: MySQL binlog events and PPP frames carry the checksum at the end. What matters is that the CRC covers the record and is verified on read. Also, Bitcask builds the whole record (CRC included) and writes it in one call rather than flushing the CRC first.
precise_version: Many log formats (Bitcask, LevelDB) put the CRC at the start of the record; others put it at the end - either works as long as the reader knows the record length and verifies the CRC before trusting the data.

note: Neither example holds. In Postgres, the commit log (pg_xact) stores transaction commit status data, not CRC'd records; in the WAL record header, xl_crc is the last field of the fixed header, after xl_tot_len, xl_xid, xl_prev, xl_info and xl_rmid. In the MySQL binlog the event header starts with a timestamp, and the CRC32 checksum is the last 4 bytes of each event. LevelDB's log and Bitcask do put the CRC first.
precise_version: Bitcask and LevelDB put the CRC at the start of each record; the Postgres WAL and the MySQL binlog also protect every record with a CRC but place it elsewhere (Postgres at the end of the record header, MySQL at the end of each event).

note: Network formats do not consistently put the CRC first: PPP carries its Frame Check Sequence at the end of the frame (as Ethernet does), and TCP's checksum sits in the middle of its header, after ports, sequence numbers and window. A receiver verifies the frame once it is complete.
precise_version: Network frames also carry checksums (often at the end, as the PPP/Ethernet FCS) so the receiver can detect corruption.

precise_version: Riak is a distributed key-value store whose default storage backend is Bitcask; Uber used it in parts of its dispatch platform around 2015.

note: Elasticsearch is more than an HTTP wrapper: each shard is a Lucene index and Elasticsearch adds distribution across nodes, replication and a REST API. The analogy works: Riak likewise runs a Bitcask per vnode and adds the distribution layer.

Riak is masterless, not master-slave: 'There is no master node; no node has more responsibilities than others', and any node can coordinate a request. It uses consistent hashing over a ring of partitions (vnodes), but data is not split into mutually exclusive sets: each object is stored on N vnodes (N configurable, e.g. 3), and Riak is eventually consistent by default. Riak keeps a separate Bitcask per vnode.
precise_version: Riak makes Bitcask distributed: a masterless ring with consistent hashing, each key replicated to N nodes, any node able to coordinate a request, and a Bitcask instance per partition underneath.

A useful heuristic but an over-generalisation: many high-throughput persistent systems do use append-only logs (WAL, commit logs), yet throughput also comes from batching, group commit, relaxed sync (e.g. Cassandra acknowledges writes before its periodic commit-log sync) and in-memory designs.

In LSM designs the memtable holds the most recent writes (keys and values) in memory, but SSTables themselves are immutable on-disk files - values are not kept in memory overall. The accurate contrast: Bitcask keeps every key in RAM and values on disk; LSM keeps only recent writes in RAM and sorted keys and values on disk, so keys need not fit in memory.
precise_version: In an LSM tree only the memtable (recent writes) is in memory; SSTables are sorted, immutable files on disk. Bitcask instead keeps every key (not values) in memory.

note: Two issues. (1) LSM engines do not lose memtable data on a crash by design: RocksDB and Cassandra write every update to a write-ahead/commit log before the memtable and replay it on restart (exposure depends only on the log sync setting). (2) Real Bitcask's default sync_strategy is 'none', which lets the OS decide when to flush; per-write durability needs o_sync. Both families trade durability against throughput through sync settings.
precise_version: Bitcask appends every write straight to its data file, while an LSM engine appends to a write-ahead log and buffers in a memtable; in both, crash durability depends on how often the log is synced to disk.

note: Personal anecdote. The paper itself exists: 'Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data' by Justin Sheehy and David Smith (Basho, 2010).

Neither POSIX nor disks promise that a small header write survives a crash whole: Postgres notes a power loss can leave some 512-byte sectors written and others not, and an unaligned header can straddle a sector. The CRC design does not need atomic headers anyway: a torn header or value simply fails the CRC check.

A ~20-byte header is unlikely to be torn, but not certain (it can straddle a sector boundary); the CRC check is what makes the design safe regardless.
